what: Western Europe (aside from elite) unfamiliar with sugar.
Sugar imported from eastern Mediterranean keeps increasing even after Crusades fail to capture 'Holy Land'.
From Levant & Egypt → eastern Mediterranean → western Mediterranean/Iberia → islands → Atlantic islands → Americas. No major technological change.
Mediterranean remodelled peasant cane producers + separate crushing/boiling + trade into integrated plantation (cultivation + crushing + boiling + refining at one site).
Two-roller horizontal mill emerges in Western India; possibly Portuguese → New World or roundabout West India→Madeira→Canary→Hispaniola.
Hand-operated presses → more efficient three-cylinder presses powered by animals → wind or water (plantations near rivers).
Barbados ~400 pairs of wings turn crushing rollers; windmills survive Industrial Revolution; 219 wind-powered Barbados sugar estates on eve of WWI.
Steam engines; better crushers; steam-powered cane crushers; movable & fixed rails; conveyor belts; Barbados wind→steam; British Guiana & Jamaica steam; transport improved.
Large open copper boiling pans + coal; 'sugar bakers'; final whitening in British/Dutch towns; clay-washing of cones; curing; loaves trimmed & wrapped; crystallization; white vs brown; 'bleaching'.
Centrifuges introduced; separation months→hours; standard even on enslaved-labour plantations.
First developed in Britain for refining imported raw cane sugar; later adopted; sealed vessels boil at lower temperature under reduced pressure; double- to quintuple-effect evaporation.
New cane varieties, incl. Otaheite strain from Pacific (Tahiti, late 1700s); planting distance, plough, drainage, irrigation, manure/fertiliser.
Timber/firewood; bagasse on Barbados; bagasse from Egyptian Mamluk precedent.

Cheap enslaved labour meant little incentive to upgrade; expanding plantation + enslaved people 'cheaper' & 'more efficient'; exception: better crushing for short ripening season; colonial tax policy blocked colonial refining.
